The [optimesh repository](https://github.com/meshpro/optimesh) directs commercial users to **support@mondaytech.com**. This supports ongoing commercialization under Monday Tech, but not a separately incorporated company called MeshPro or a completed acquisition. No funding amount or valuation was located. I retained the supplied entity label and flagged the identity issue rather than inventing a buyer or acquisition event.

### 11. Yunnan BinaryStars Technologies

**Status: private, operating.** The company's [About page](https://www.binarystarstech.com/en/about/) describes its integrated hardware and software engineering business and links the Borneo-IoT product line. The [Borneo-IoT app terms](https://www.borneoiot.com/app/tos/), updated March 2026, identify the service as “operated by Yunnan BinaryStars Technologies, Co., Ltd.”

No disclosed equity amount, valuation or acquisition price was found. The terms retain some unfilled template placeholders elsewhere; I used only their explicit operator identification, corroborated by the company website.

## Uncertain rows and interpretation

The principal uncertainties are **OtterMind**'s corporate relationship to the Chinese Chat2DB business; **HeroUI**'s conflicting unsupported funding totals; **Usablica**'s and **MeshPro**'s legal-entity identities; **LiteFold**'s ambiguous round descriptions; and **Textualize**'s exact cessation date. Chatwoot's reported database total also conflicts with its own disclosure. None of these uncertainties was resolved by inventing a number.

No qualifying post-money valuation, completed acquisition price, or first-day public-market capitalization was verified for these companies. Consequently, every valuation and exit-value field is blank. No currency conversion was necessary for the accepted funding figures.

## Saved files and reproduction

All files below concern the public-disclosure snapshot as of 2026-11-26; genome builds and scientific dataset releases are not applicable.

- `/workspace/downloads/oss_financial_disclosures/financial_disclosures.csv`: Analysis-ready curated data. Sources are the company, investor and news URLs above. Transformations were entity matching, status classification, exclusion of grants and uncompleted offers, and conversion of explicit USD million amounts into integer USD digits. Validated for 11 rows, exact columns, integer-or-blank financial fields and notes of at most 25 words.
- `/workspace/downloads/oss_financial_disclosures/evidence.json`: Supporting original tool-returned search and fetched-page text, all retrieval queries and URLs, and used-source metadata. Retrieval used `e14c.web.web_search` with five results per query and `e14c.web.fetch_parsed_page` on the recorded HTTPS URLs. Results were serialized without financial estimation.
- `/workspace/downloads/oss_financial_disclosures/sources.bib`: Supporting hand-curated bibliographic metadata for the 29 sources cited below. Source URLs and publication dates are retained when available.
- `/workspace/downloads/oss_financial_disclosures/methodology.json`: Supporting research parameters, screening definitions, conflicts, call counts and validation findings. Derived from the saved evidence and curation decisions.
- `/workspace/downloads/oss_financial_disclosures/reproduce_retrieval.py`: Repeats the exact retrieval calls recorded in `evidence.json`; run with `python /workspace/downloads/oss_financial_disclosures/reproduce_retrieval.py`. It does not substitute automated extraction for the documented manual financial judgments.

The same bibliography was also saved through `save_citation` to `/workspace/citations/default_project/08d1321c-1746-402b-bad9-7f630a43bf59.bib`. Complete bibliography follows so the caller does not need filesystem access.

outputs.text:
# Financial details of companies built on popular open-source projects

Part of a pre-registered study (issue #380). The companies in your input were already classified as `core`: their
main paid product is an open-source project they lead, in another form (hosted service, open-core or enterprise
edition, paid licences or support, or hardware). Your job is to find what each company raised, what it was or is
worth, and what happened to it, **with a source URL for every number**.

## Input

A CSV with one row per company: `owner` (GitHub login), `entity` (company name from the classification),
`parent` (current owner if acquired, when known), `country`, `basis`, `status_hint`, `stars` (the org's stars in
the frame) and the top repositories. Rows with `h9_addition=1` are companies that built the project and later
handed it to a foundation (e.g. Anyscale and Ray); research the company named in `entity`, not the foundation.
Several GitHub orgs can belong to one company (e.g. Docker Inc. owns `docker` and `moby`); fill each row anyway.

## For each company, find

| Column | What | Rules |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `status` | One of `listed`, `acquired`, `private`, `shut_down`, `unknown` | `listed` = its own shares trade today. `acquired` = bought by another company (even if it still operates as a subsidiary, or was later taken private by PE: use `acquired` and say so in notes). `shut_down` = ceased operating, wound down, or sold only its assets/IP in distress. `private` = independent and operating |
| `status_date` | YYYY or YYYY-MM of the listing, acquisition or shutdown | |
| `ticker` | Yahoo Finance ticker if listed (e.g. `ESTC`, `MDB`, `9988.HK`) | |
| `acquirer` | Buyer if acquired | |
| `exit_value_usd` | Disclosed acquisition price (equity or enterprise value as reported), in USD | Blank if undisclosed. Don't use "reportedly" figures unless no official figure exists; then say "reported" in notes |
| `exit_source` | URL | |
| `total_funding_usd` | Total disclosed equity funding raised before listing/exit or to date, in USD | From the company's or investors' announcements, or a reputable news report summing them. Exclude debt where you can tell |
| `funding_asof` | YYYY-MM of the latest round counted | |
| `funding_source` | URL | |
| `last_valuation_usd` | Latest disclosed post-money valuation if private; blank otherwise | |
| `valuation_date` | YYYY-MM | |
| `valuation_source` | URL | |
| `peak_value_usd` | Highest value ever disclosed: any private post-money valuation, the market cap at the close of its first trading day, or exit value | |
| `peak_value_date` | YYYY-MM | |
| `peak_source` | URL | |
| `ever_1b` | `yes` if any disclosed value reached USD 1B (private mark, first-day market cap, or exit price); `no` if the company's disclosed values are all below 1B or it never disclosed one and is clearly small; `unknown` otherwise | |
| `legal_name` | The US legal entity name if the company is (or was) US-incorporated, e.g. "Grafana Labs, Inc." or "Raintank, Inc." (the name it would use on an SEC Form D). Several names separated by `|` | |
| `notes` | ≤ 25 words: anything an investor should know (down round, relicensing, acqui-hire, crypto token, numbers that conflict between sources) | |

## How to work

- Use WebSearch and WebFetch. Good sources: company press releases and blogs, investor (VC) announcements, SEC
  filings (EDGAR), Reuters, TechCrunch, Bloomberg, The Information (summaries), Wikipedia only for its cited
  sources. Crunchbase pages are often blocked; don't rely on them.
- **Every number needs a URL that states it.** If you know a figure from memory but can't find a page stating it,
  leave the number blank and put "memory: ~$XM" in notes.
- Spend about 3–5 searches or fetches per company at most. Small companies with no disclosed rounds are common:
  record `status` and leave the numbers blank. Absence of disclosure is itself data.
- Convert non-USD amounts at the rate near the announcement date and say so in notes.
- Don't skip companies that failed or that are tiny. Those rows matter most.

## Output

Write a CSV with a header to the path in your task, one row per input company, in input order, with columns:

`owner,entity,status,status_date,ticker,acquirer,exit_value_usd,exit_source,total_funding_usd,funding_asof,funding_source,last_valuation_usd,valuation_date,valuation_source,peak_value_usd,peak_value_date,peak_source,ever_1b,legal_name,notes`

Numbers as plain digits in USD (e.g. 6400000000), no "$", "B" or commas. Quote fields containing commas. Save
progress after every ~10 companies. When done, reply with the row count, counts by status, and any rows you are
unsure about.

## About OpenCode

OpenCode is an open-source AI coding agent that developers run from a terminal, a desktop app, an IDE extension or the web, with the AI model of their choice. Its code is open under the MIT licence. The product is made by Anomaly, whose website also lists Rebase, a live trivia project, and Antarctica, a bike challenge.

According to TechFundingNews in January 2026, Jay V is chief executive and Frank Wang is chief technology officer. The two met at the University of Waterloo and launched Anomaly together. Dax Raad, an early user of their open-source framework SST who joined in 2021, and Adam Elmore joined them as co-founders when OpenCode launched on 19 June. SST went through Y Combinator in 2021, raised USD 1 million after demo day, reached 25,000 GitHub stars and became profitable in 2025, the article said.

OpenCode's website says the tool loads language servers automatically and can run several agents in parallel on one project. It connects to more than 75 model providers through the Models.dev database, including local models,. OpenCode Zen is a curated set of models the team has tested for coding agents, sold pay-as-you-go at provider prices. OpenCode Enterprise adds central configuration, single sign-on and an internal AI gateway, with per-seat pricing. The company says it does not store code or context data unless the free models are used, and its Trust Center lists SOC 2 Type 2 compliance.

TechFundingNews reported 650,000 monthly active users and 50,000 GitHub stars about five months after launch, with 500 contributors and annualised revenue of several million dollars, mostly from Zen. It named Cloudflare as an enterprise user. The website states more than 215,000 GitHub stars, 950 contributors and more than 16 million developers a month.

TechFundingNews said OpenCode raised an undisclosed funding round within months of launching, without an amount or investors.

# We raised $8 Million to bring Kilo Speed to Agentic Engineering

Scott Breitenother

Dec 10, 2025

Today we announced that Kilo Code has raised $8m in seed funding. The funding round was led by Cota Capital with participation from Breakers, General Catalyst, Quiet Capital, and Tokyo Black. This is an exciting moment for us and I want to pause and share why I am personally so energized about Kilo.

My last venture was building Brooklyn Data, a consultancy that helped companies unlock the value of their data. I started Brooklyn Data in 2018 and we rode a wave that was far bigger than we were: companies adopting cloud data warehouses like Snowflake, the modern data stack including dbt, and the rise of analytics engineering. It was an incredible moment. The foundational technology changed, the culture of data changed, and those two changes created a cascading effect that 10xed the impact of data work.

Thanks for reading Kilo Blog! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

After I sold Brooklyn Data and stepped back from the company a year later, I had a nagging feeling: Would I ever again have a front row seat to such a great moment of change?

And as if right on cue, I was introduced to my cofounder Sid (co-founder, exec chair, and former CEO of GitLab) by a mutual friend. We both saw the incredible potential of AI to make every developer in the world dramatically more productive, as well as the frustrations with available AI coding tools. We had to do something about it (more on that below).

Since launching earlier this year, Kilo has gone from 0 to 750,000+ downloads, risen to #1 on OpenRouter, and is processing over 6 trillion tokens monthly. In October, we launched a Teams plan, followed two weeks later by an Enterprise plan. In the last month we have released parallel agents, one-click deploy, code review, autocomplete, managed indexing, and app builder. Thousands of developers are using these features today, and loving them.

This pace would have been unheard of even a year ago, but agentic engineering has enabled us to move faster than ever before. We call this Kilo Speed.

We’re fighting AI drag

# Kilo acquired by Anaconda

### The Deal

Anaconda, the Python-platform company used by some 52 million developers, has acquired Kilo Code, an agentic-coding startup whose gateway routes AI engineering work across hundreds of models; terms were not disclosed. 1 Kilo Code orchestrates roughly 10 trillion tokens a month for more than three million developers, routing across 500-plus open-weight and frontier models with agent orchestration and enterprise analytics layered on top. 1 

Kilo, led by co-founder and chief executive Scott Breitenother, sells enterprises a way out of a bind that AI coding tools created: sprawling, unmonitored spend across personal accounts and single-vendor lock-in. 1 Its model gateway lets a company route each task to the cheapest capable model — early customers report 30-50% cuts in token consumption — while keeping visibility and governance over where code and data go. 1 

For Anaconda, the acquisition extends its franchise from managing Python packages and environments into managing AI model access — the same "trusted foundation" pitch, one layer up. 2 Anaconda already sits between enterprises and open-source software supply chains; Kilo lets it sit between enterprises and the models, governing spend and data flow the way it governs packages.

The logic is that governance, not raw capability, is where the enterprise AI money is. Frontier-model quality is converging and commoditising; what large organisations will pay for is a control plane — visibility into spend, a hedge against any single vendor, and an audit trail for where data went. Anaconda built a business by being the trusted intermediary for open-source Python, and buying Kilo is a bet that it can be the same intermediary for model access, with the routing layer — not any one model — as the durable position. Paying an undisclosed sum for a company already moving 10 trillion tokens a month suggests it wanted that position before the layer commoditises too.

# We raised $8 Million to bring Kilo Speed to Agentic Engineering

Scott Breitenother

Dec 10, 2025

Today we announced that Kilo Code has raised $8m in seed funding. The funding round was led by Cota Capital with participation from Breakers, General Catalyst, Quiet Capital, and Tokyo Black. This is an exciting moment for us and I want to pause and share why I am personally so energized about Kilo.

My last venture was building Brooklyn Data, a consultancy that helped companies unlock the value of their data. I started Brooklyn Data in 2018 and we rode a wave that was far bigger than we were: companies adopting cloud data warehouses like Snowflake, the modern data stack including dbt, and the rise of analytics engineering. It was an incredible moment. The foundational technology changed, the culture of data changed, and those two changes created a cascading effect that 10xed the impact of data work.

Thanks for reading Kilo Blog! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

After I sold Brooklyn Data and stepped back from the company a year later, I had a nagging feeling: Would I ever again have a front row seat to such a great moment of change?

And as if right on cue, I was introduced to my cofounder Sid (co-founder, exec chair, and former CEO of GitLab) by a mutual friend. We both saw the incredible potential of AI to make every developer in the world dramatically more productive, as well as the frustrations with available AI coding tools. We had to do something about it (more on that below).

Since launching earlier this year, Kilo has gone from 0 to 750,000+ downloads, risen to #1 on OpenRouter, and is processing over 6 trillion tokens monthly. In October, we launched a Teams plan, followed two weeks later by an Enterprise plan. In the last month we have released parallel agents, one-click deploy, code review, autocomplete, managed indexing, and app builder. Thousands of developers are using these features today, and loving them.

This pace would have been unheard of even a year ago, but agentic engineering has enabled us to move faster than ever before. We call this Kilo Speed.

We’re fighting AI drag

The AI coding landscape is maturing incredibly fast. Gartner is two years into the Magic Quadrant for AI Coding Assistants. There are many companies throwing their hat in the agentic development ring—from pure plays to foundational labs and hyperscalers.

Why Kilo? We believe engineers deserve better. With AI coding, engineers should be moving faster than ever, but tools like Cursor and GitHub Copilot are introducing AI drag, artificial friction that slows down development. Downgraded models, rate limiting, and model lock-in create a new breed of frustrations for engineers. Overage fees, limits on “premium requests”, and pricing that requires a PhD to decipher—other agentic development tools have more fine print than a used-car warranty. It ends up feeling like these tools are working against you, rather than with you.

And it’s all intentionally designed to be confusing so that you spend more money or don’t get the value of what you paid for. They’re selling gym memberships, hoping that you don’t actually show up to work out (and then charging you extra when you do).

We’re also seeing other platforms lock developers into an unnecessarily limited number of models. This seems absurd when new models launch every week; we know, we launched three last week. You shouldn’t have to choose between the latest frontier model, the ultra low latency open source model, and the extremely cost effective model from an upstart model lab. Everything in AI moves so quickly that anchoring yourself to a fixed set of models is a recipe for falling behind. Kilo has over 500 models and counting, including models from OpenAI, Anthropic, xAI, and Mistral AI. You’ll always have the best model for the job, and it never costs more than the list price of the lab.

Building for Kilo Speed

We’re bringing Kilo Speed to agentic engineering with an all-in-one platform that accelerates every single person on your team.

Anaconda built a business by being the trusted intermediary for open-source Python, and buying Kilo is a bet that it can be the same intermediary for model access, with the routing layer — not any one model — as the durable position. Paying an undisclosed sum for a company already moving 10 trillion tokens a month suggests it wanted that position before the layer commoditises too.

4:25 AM PDT · October 7, 2024

Fledgling fintech startup OpenBB is revealing the next step in its plans to take on the heavyweights of the investment research world. The company is launching a new, free version of a product that will open its arsenal of data and financial tooling to more users.

OpenBB is the handiwork of software engineer Didier Lopes, who launched the Python-based platform back in 2021 as a way for amateur investors and enthusiasts to do investment research using different datasets for free, via a command line interface (CLI). The company went on to raise $8.5 million in seed funding from OSS Capital and angel investors such as Ram Shriram, an early backer of Google.

While the community-based, open source project has amassed some 50,000 users, OpenBB has also been building an enterprise incarnation called Terminal Pro. This paid version gives teams access to an interface, pre-built database integrations, an Excel add-in, and various security and support bolt-ons that would appeal to larger businesses.

OpenBB claims some big-name customers that include shipping and logistics company Pangaea Logistics Solutions and an unnamed investment firm, which Lopes says has $6.4 billion in assets under management.

However, OpenBB is now looking to attract the kinds of customers that might otherwise be tempted to check out Bloomberg Terminal or products from upstarts like AI market intelligence startup AlphaSense, which raised at a $4 billion valuation in June 2024.

## Terminal velocity

The all-new OpenBB Terminal — not to be confused with the previous CLI-based OpenBB Terminal that the startup sunsetted in March — is a full-fledged web app, though it strips out many of the premium features of Terminal Pro. It’s fully customizable, can run on any operating system or platform, and provides access to an AI-enabled OpenBB copilot. Like the previous OpenBB Terminal, the all-new web app is also free to use.

OpenBB Terminal is perhaps something of a middle ground between the CLI centricity of the open source project and the bells-and-whistles feature set of the enterprise product.

Today, we’re sharing a difficult update. OpenBB is winding down as a company. At the same time, we are committing to release the OpenBB product suite under a permissive open-source license.

That includes OpenBB Workspace, OpenBB Copilot, OpenBB Excel Add-in, and Open Data Platform.

OpenBB began as an open-source project built to give people and firms more control over their investment-research environments. Over the past five years, it grew into products used across financial data, research workflows, AI, and an ecosystem of applications created by our partners and community.

We were not able to build a sustainable business around that vision. But the technology the team built should not disappear.

The open-source releases will allow developers, data providers, individuals, and financial institutions to use, modify, deploy, and build on the OpenBB stack. We are still finalizing the release order, license details, repository structure, and long-term stewardship of each project. We will share more as that work is completed.

def cite_result(label,i,why=''):
 x=searches[label]['results'][i];url=x['url']
 if url not in used:
  key='audit'+str(len(used)+1)
  title=x['title'].replace('&',r'\&').replace('%',r'\%').replace('_',r'\_').replace('#',r'\#')
  from urllib.parse import urlparse
  author=urlparse(url).netloc
  bib=f'@online{{{key},\n author = {{{{{author}}}}},\n title = {{{title}}},\n url = {{{url}}},\n urldate = {{2026-11-26}},\n'
  date=x.get('publishedDate')
  if date:bib+=f' date = {{{date[:10]}}},\n'
  bib+='}\n';save_citation(bib)
  used[url]={**x,'use':why,'key':key}
  Path('audit_work/used_sources.json').write_text(json.dumps(used,indent=2,default=str))
 return url

# the tiny corp raised $5.1M

 May 24, 2023 

Here we go again. I started another company. The money is in the bank.

### What is the tiny corp?

The tiny corp is a computer company. We sell computers for more than they cost to make; I’ve been thinking about this one for a while. In the limit, it’s a chip company, but there’s a lot of intermediates along the way.

The human brain has about 20 PFLOPS of compute. I’ve written various blog posts about this. Sadly, 20 PFLOPS of compute is not accessible to most people, costing about $1M to buy or $100/hr to rent.

With the way AI is going, we risk large entities controlling the majority of the compute in the world. I do not want “I think there’s a world market for maybe five computers.” to ever be the world we live in.

The goal of the tiny corp is: “to commoditize the petaflop”

### What is tinygrad?

I started tinygrad in Oct 2020. It started as a toy project to teach me about neural networks, it’s now carved out a good niche in the inference space running the model in openpilot, and soon will be a serious competitor to PyTorch in many places.

The main advantage is in the tinygrad IR. It has 12 operations, all of which are ADD/MUL only. `x[3]` is supported, `x[y]` is not. Matrix multiplies and convolutions are just multiplies and sums, surrounded by a bunch of zero cost movement operations (like reshape, permute, expand).

```python
# a fast matmul in tinygrad (a@b works also of course)
from tinygrad.tensor import Tensor
N = 2048; a, b = Tensor.randn(N,N), Tensor.randn(N,N)
c = (a.reshape(N,1,N) * b.permute(1,0).reshape(1,N,N)).sum(axis=2)
```

tinygrad is lazy, like Haskell, to allow op fusion without the user ever having to think about it.

### Ok, so?

The current crop of AI chip companies failed. Many of them managed to tape out chips, some of those chips even worked. But not a single one wrote a decent framework to use those chips. They had similar performance/$ to NVIDIA, and way worse software. Of course they failed. Everyone just bought stuff from NVIDIA.

I think the only way to start an AI chip company is to start with the software. The computing in ML is not general purpose computing. 95% of models in use today (including LLMs and image generation) have all their compute and memory accesses statically computable.

Continue is an open-source AI coding platform that has repositioned from an IDE assistant into "quality control for your software factory" — source-controlled AI checks that run on every pull request, enforceable in CI and powered by the open-source Continue CLI. ## Product Overview

Continue's flagship product as of mid-2026 is AI checks: markdown files stored in `.continue/checks/` in your repo, each containing a name, description, and prompt. On every pull request, Continue evaluates the diff against each check and reports results as native GitHub status checks — green for pass, red for fail with suggested fixes. The pitch is "consistency over breadth": mechanically enforcing the standards your team writes down rather than offering broad, unpredictable AI review feedback.

The interactive tools remain: the open-source CLI agent (`cn`) — the same agent that powers the IDE extensions — and VS Code/JetBrains extensions for chat, edit, autocomplete, and agent mode.

# Spain backs open-source design tool Penpot in €6.9M round

● Jul 2026

What's the deal? Kaleidos, the Madrid company behind open-source interface design platform Penpot, has raised €6.9 million in an early VC round. The Sociedad Española para la Transformación Tecnológica (SETT), a public body under Spain's Ministry for Digital Transformation and the Civil Service, contributed €1.92 million.

What does Penpot do? It is an open-source platform for designing and building user interfaces. Its pitch: the first design tool serving both designers and developers, treating design as code — a structure it says suits generative AI natively.

Why now? The most-used interface design platform is controlled by a single US company that holds designs, data, and development considered sensitive intellectual property. SETT frames its investment as a push for European technological sovereignty in a field dependent on foreign firms.

What's the endgame? The funding will let Kaleidos scale its commercial team and paid product. SETT made the investment through its Next Tech facility, using money from Spain's Recovery, Transformation and Resilience Plan, drawn from the EU's Next Generation funds.

Track record: Founded in 2011, Kaleidos has built technology for clients including Inditex, Decathlon, Scotland Yard, and the University of Lausanne. Penpot itself emerged from an internal hackathon; the team is 60% women.

"El Gobierno de España apuesta por la soberanía digital europea, el talento patrio y el código abierto," said Óscar López, minister for digital transformation and the civil service, adding that the government backed Kaleidos for both its innovation and its 15-year track record.

The signal: At €6.9 million, the round sits in the 92nd percentile of all-time early VC deals in Spanish enterprise software, based on 161 comparable rounds. It reflects growing state appetite to fund open-source alternatives to dominant US software platforms.

# the tiny corp raised $5.1M

 May 24, 2023 

Here we go again. I started another company. The money is in the bank.

### What is the tiny corp?

The tiny corp is a computer company. We sell computers for more than they cost to make; I’ve been thinking about this one for a while. In the limit, it’s a chip company, but there’s a lot of intermediates along the way.

The human brain has about 20 PFLOPS of compute. I’ve written various blog posts about this. Sadly, 20 PFLOPS of compute is not accessible to most people, costing about $1M to buy or $100/hr to rent.

With the way AI is going, we risk large entities controlling the majority of the compute in the world. I do not want “I think there’s a world market for maybe five computers.” to ever be the world we live in.

The goal of the tiny corp is: “to commoditize the petaflop”

### What is tinygrad?

I started tinygrad in Oct 2020. It started as a toy project to teach me about neural networks, it’s now carved out a good niche in the inference space running the model in openpilot, and soon will be a serious competitor to PyTorch in many places.

The main advantage is in the tinygrad IR. It has 12 operations, all of which are ADD/MUL only. `x[3]` is supported, `x[y]` is not. Matrix multiplies and convolutions are just multiplies and sums, surrounded by a bunch of zero cost movement operations (like reshape, permute, expand).

The pitch is "consistency over breadth": mechanically enforcing the standards your team writes down rather than offering broad, unpredictable AI review feedback.

# the tiny corp raised $5.1M

 May 24, 2023 

Here we go again. I started another company. The money is in the bank.

### What is the tiny corp?

The tiny corp is a computer company. We sell computers for more than they cost to make; I’ve been thinking about this one for a while. In the limit, it’s a chip company, but there’s a lot of intermediates along the way.

The human brain has about 20 PFLOPS of compute. I’ve written various blog posts about this. Sadly, 20 PFLOPS of compute is not accessible to most people, costing about $1M to buy or $100/hr to rent.

With the way AI is going, we risk large entities controlling the majority of the compute in the world. I do not want “I think there’s a world market for maybe five computers.” to ever be the world we live in.

The goal of the tiny corp is: “to commoditize the petaflop”

### What is tinygrad?

I started tinygrad in Oct 2020. It started as a toy project to teach me about neural networks, it’s now carved out a good niche in the inference space running the model in openpilot, and soon will be a serious competitor to PyTorch in many places.

The main advantage is in the tinygrad IR. It has 12 operations, all of which are ADD/MUL only. `x[3]` is supported, `x[y]` is not. Matrix multiplies and convolutions are just multiplies and sums, surrounded by a bunch of zero cost movement operations (like reshape, permute, expand).


# Coder

October 23, 2026| 25 min

A report from Contrary Research. Discover Coder's founding story, product, business model, and an in-depth analysis of the business.

## Thesis

Artificial intelligence writes a growing share of the world's software. Claude Code went from a research preview in February 2025 to writing 4% of all public GitHub commits by February 2026. Enterprises saw similar growth in adoption. In April 2026, 75% of all new code at Google was AI-generated and approved by engineers, up from 50% in fall 2025 and more than 25% in October 2024.

Source: SemiAnalysis

As the volume of AI-written code has grown, so has the autonomy of the tools producing it. Coding agents such as Claude Code and Codex, rather than merely suggesting code, can read files, write code, run shell commands, and call tools without stopping for approval. While this autonomy improves the speed at which developers work, it also means fewer opportunities for a human to catch an error prior to execution.

For example, in a controlled study of 1.1K paid professional testers published in August 2026, the testers caught a deliberately planted dangerous command only 13.6% of the time. Anthropic’s auto mode caught 89% of the same commands, which still lets roughly one in ten through. Examples of incidents that have resulted have included agents deleting remote git branches and uploading authentication tokens.

Enterprises have struggled to put AI projects into production. In a 2025 survey of AI projects, the share of companies abandoning most AI initiatives before production rose from 17% to 42% year over year, with cost, data privacy, and security among the top obstacles respondents cited. For coding agents, both cost and risk control depend on how many tokens each agent generates and which systems it can reach. For coding agents, the binding constraint on enterprise adoption is moving from how well an agent writes code to how completely an organization can control the cost and risk of agentic implementation.

# Penpot, the open source platform for designers and their coders, draws up $12M as users jump to 250K

[Ingrid Lunden](https://techcrunch.com/author/ingrid-lunden/)

5:08 AM PST · February 2, 2023

Open source projects continue to stand out as compelling alternatives to proprietary software for those who are looking for more flexibility or price leverage in the tools that they use to work. Today one of the juggernauts in the space of design is announcing some funding. [Penpot](https://penpot.app/), an open source platform for designers and developers to collaborate on work in a single environment, has raised $12 million, equity funding that it will use to drive more adoption after hitting 250,000 users this month and 20,000 “stars” on GitHub.

For some context on those numbers, Penpot’s user numbers blew up last year in the wake of [Adobe acquiring Figma for $20 billion](https://techcrunch.com/2022/09/15/adobe-is-buying-figma-for-20b-taking-out-one-of-its-biggest-rivals-in-digital-design/), growing 5,600% to 100,000 users in the span of a couple of weeks. That momentum is still strong if not quite as outsized: Penpot’s 250,000 users today represent a user growth rate of 500%.

“The battleground in design for the next few years is clear and that is who will win over the developers,” said Pablo Ruiz-Múzquiz, Penpot’s CEO and co-founder, in an interview this week.

The logic behind Penpot has been to create tools that designers will use and love but that will be equally embraced by their developer counterparts, too — an audience that design tools up to now have failed to capture, let alone build for or target, yet is essential to include in the collaboration process earlier than it typically is. “Developers outnumber designers 10 to 1. So while Figma has 1 million accounts, those are just designers, which means they have cut out an important audience. Sure, we want more designers in the world, but we keep getting more developers.” Building something both can use at the same time, he said, “is the big opportunity for Penpot.”

The funding will be used in part to build out more tools that can be used both in the cloud and in self-hosted and local environments; indeed, the news is coinciding with Penpot launching a number of these out of beta that speak to how it’s building with design and coding sensibilities in tandem.

They include a new suite of “Flex Layout” tools for building responsive layouts in CSS, a tool that lets users tap browser memory to boost memory caches for collaborative projects up to 16 GB (2 GB has been an industry standard limit up to now); better code inspection features; more agility for adding in occasional contributors to a project; and more.

All of these, as with all of Penpot, are totally free to use as the company has yet to put in place any kind of paid features or services. The longer-term questions, therefore, are not just if Penpot can continue to pick up a critical mass of users of its open source tools, but if it can find effective ways of monetizing the platform to keep them there.

# Cursor quietly acquires Continue, an open-source alternative to GitHub Copilot

Cursor acquires Continue, the open-source AI coding assistant with 34K GitHub stars, in a quiet acqui-hire that shuts down the product and hands the codebase to the community.

Jun 22nd, 2026 3:48pm by   [Paul Sawers](https://thenewstack.io/author/paul-sawers/ "Posts by Paul Sawers")

![Featued image for: Cursor quietly acquires Continue, an open-source alternative to GitHub Copilot](https://cdn.thenewstack.io/media/2026/06/901c854e-eduardo-ramos-2u7juh5refc-unsplash-1-1024x683.jpg "width=1024 | height=683")

Eduardo Ramos for Unsplash+

The AI developer tools consolidation continues apace, with news that Cursor has snapped up open-source coding assistant [Continue](https://www.continue.dev/) — its latest acquisition in a busy 18 months.

The deal itself seems to have been completed around the same time SpaceX confirmed it was [doling out $60 billion for Cursor](https://thenewstack.io/spacex-cursor-ai-coding/), meaning that Elon Musk’s rocket juggernaut is now the owner of Continue as well.

Terms of the deal haven’t been disclosed and, in truth, there hasn’t been much of an announcement to speak of. Around June 16, Continue updated its homepage with a brief message stating that it has been bought by Cursor, and an accompanying FAQ explaining that existing users have until July 15 to export their data before it’s deleted, and that recurring billing has been disabled.

Continue, it seems, has been discontinued.

![Cursor has acquired Continue](https://cdn.thenewstack.io/media/2026/06/732deb7f-acquiredzz-1024x701.png "width=1024 | height=701")

**Cursor has acquired Continue**

Confirmation also arrived via online reports from developers [who received emails](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=48580219) from Continue about their accounts, and via LinkedIn, where [Matthaus Krzykowski](https://www.linkedin.com/in/matthauskrzykowski/) — an angel investor in Continue through Angel Invest and a long-time collaborator via his data pipeline company [dltHub](https://dlthub.com/) — posted a personal tribute to the founding team, which includes [Ty Dunn](https://www.linkedin.com/in/tylerjdunn/) and [Nate Sesti](https://www.linkedin.com/in/natesesti/).

Krzykowski says that he’s tracked Dunn’s career since 2019, when he was the first product manager at Berlin-based [conversational AI company Rasa](https://techcrunch.com/2024/02/14/rasa-an-enterprise-focused-dev-platform-for-conversational-genai-raises-30m/). Dunn went on to become a founding engineer at dltHub in 2022 before leaving the following year to co-found Continue with Sesti. For Krzykowski, the conventional wisdom [that GitHub Copilot](https://github.blog/news-insights/product-news/introducing-github-copilot-ai-pair-programmer/) had already sewn up the market was wide of the mark — the developer experience was still badly broken.

> “2023 was still very early days of coding agents – yet most investors thought GitHub Copilot had already won.”

“2023 was still very early days of coding agents — yet most investors thought GitHub Copilot had already won,” Krzykowski [writes](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/matthauskrzykowski_continue-acquired-by-cursor-has-been-acquired-share-7474561438162829312-7oig/). “Back then, developers were stuck copy-pasting from ChatGPT and guessing what context Copilot used to make a suggestion. It was obvious there had to be a better way. Backing Ty and Nate was easy – I often bet on the people I’ve watched build up close.”

## The open-source alternative

A graduate of [Y Combinator’s Summer 2023 cohort](https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/continue), Continue [positioned itself](https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/J6f-continue-the-easiest-way-to-code-with-any-llm) as the open-source alternative to the proprietary coding assistants flooding the market. Available as a VS Code extension, JetBrains plugin, and CLI, it let developers connect any AI model of their choosing and pull in context from their own tools — Jira, Confluence, and such like — to build customized coding assistants tailored to their specific environment.

The data control angle was central to the pitch — in a market dominated by closed-source tools that developers had little visibility into, Continue was positioning itself as the transparent alternative. Speaking to TechCrunch [in early 2025](https://techcrunch.com/2025/02/26/continue-wants-to-help-developers-create-and-share-custom-ai-coding-assistants/) to mark the startup’s $3 million seed round, Dunn spelled out what that meant.

“When you use Continue, you get to keep your data,” Dunn said at the time. “As an organization, you can pool all of your data for all of your developers in one place. That is not possible in the one-size-fits-all, black box code assistant, where their SaaS offerings and strategy is to take your data and use it to improve it for everyone.”

Fast-forward 16 months, and that same startup has now been absorbed by one of the best-known proprietary players in AI coding tools. By the time of its acquisition, [Continue had accumulated](https://github.com/continuedev/continue) 34,300 GitHub stars and 4,800 forks, and raised in the region of $5 million. The team pushed a final 2.0.0 release before closing up shop — removing telemetry and tidying the code, designed as part of a deliberate handoff to the community. Under its Apache 2.0 license, the codebase remains publicly available for anyone to fork and build on.

## Cursor’s quiet consolidation

The Continue acquisition is one of two Cursor-related stories that appear to have been buried beneath the big-bucks SpaceX news. At the same time, [Cursor unveiled Origin](https://thenewstack.io/cursor-origin-github-disruption/) at its Compile developer conference — an agent-native challenger to GitHub for code hosting and collaboration that similarly flew under the radar.

Moreover, it’s the latest move in what has become a steady acquisition drumbeat for Cursor over the past 18 months, [including AI coding assistant Supermaven](https://cursor.com/blog/supermaven) and [code review startup Graphite](https://cursor.com/blog/graphite). Unlike Graphite, which has continued to operate as an independent product, the Continue deal has the hallmarks of an acqui-hire — the product appears to have been shuttered, with little public information on who from the Continue team will be making the move to Cursor.

According to Krzykowski, co-founder Nate Sesti is joining Cursor. [Dunn’s LinkedIn profile](https://www.linkedin.com/in/tylerjdunn/), meanwhile, suggests he departed Continue in May, a few weeks before the acquisition was made public, and it’s not clear whether he will be making the move to Cursor. [Chad Metcalf](https://www.linkedin.com/in/chadmetcalf/), who replaced Dunn as CEO [in April 2025](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/chadmetcalf_im-excited-to-join-continue-as-ceo-after-activity-7330627587196575746-a1gY/), hasn’t made any public announcement about his next move. Two of Continue’s founding engineers, [Dallin Romney](https://www.linkedin.com/in/romneyda/) and [Patrick Erichsen](https://www.linkedin.com/in/patrick-erichsen/), have joined [OpenClaw](https://openclaw.ai/) — the open-source AI agent that went viral earlier this year before its [creator joined OpenAI](https://steipete.me/posts/2026/openclaw) — as members of technical staff.

*The New Stack* has reached out to both Cursor and Continue for comment and will update this piece if or when we hear back.

# We Raised $50M to Build Composable Vector Search as Core Infrastructure

By Andre Zayarni, March 12, 2026

Today we're announcing $50 million in Series B funding, led by AVP, with participation from Bosch Ventures, Unusual Ventures, Spark Capital, and 42CAP.

### Retrieval Is on the Critical Path of Every AI System

Every serious AI workload — RAG, agents, multimodal search — depends on retrieving the right information, at the right time, under real constraints. Teams prototype with whatever is convenient, then hit walls in production: indexes that stall under writes, filtering applied after search instead of during it, tail latencies that spike under load. These aren't configuration problems. They're architectural ones. And they're why we started Qdrant.

Our design philosophy: we are building fundamental infrastructure. The kind that lasts years, maybe decades. Think Linux kernel, not SaaS wrapper. That conviction is why Qdrant is built from the ground up in Rust — because infrastructure on the critical path of production AI cannot afford garbage collection pauses, memory safety issues, or the performance unpredictability of managed runtimes. It's why we control the stack down to assembly, rebuilding any layer that doesn't meet the standard. And it's why Qdrant delivers predictable low tail latency at billion-scale, running consistently from edge devices to bare-metal supercomputers like Aurora at Argonne National Laboratory.

 Tile.ai Team 

The company becomes Tile.ai and introduces a governed AI data layer that helps organizations safely use sensitive data with AI — wherever it lives.

Portainer is a series A company based in Auckland (New Zealand), founded in 2017 by Neil Cresswell and Anthony Lapenna. # MEDIA RELEASE: Portainer.io Closes US$6.2 Million Funding Round

June 22, 2022 · Neil Cresswell

Portainer.io today announced it has closed a US$6.2 million funding round. The round, which is an extension of its Series A that closed in May 2021, is led by Movac and backed by all the Series A investors (Sonae IM/Bright Pixel, Bessemer Venture Partners, BlackNova, AltVentures). It also adds US investor Shasta Ventures and New Zealand Growth Capital Partners to the roster as interest in the company grows.

Portainer launched in 2017 as an open source product to simplify the management of Docker and Swarm environments. In August 2020, it added support for enterprise Kubernetes, which is becoming the de facto industry standard for orchestrating containerized environments. By adding support for both Kubernetes and HashiCorp’s Nomad, Portainer has become the only universal container management system that works from the data centre to the edge and has been recognized by CRN.com as one of the 10 hottest Kubernetes startups of 2022.

Mermaid is an AI-powered diagramming and text-to-chart tool that allows users to build flowcharts, sequence diagrams, and more with AI, code, or visual editor. Most teams building complex systems hit the same wall: the diagram lives in one place, the code lives in another, and neither stays current for long.

Mermaid diagrams are text, so they version with your code, travel with your PRs, and can be read, generated, and acted on by every major AI platform, including Claude Code, Cursor, ChatGPT, Gemini, GitHub, and more. 200k+ teams use Mermaid as the layer where complex systems stay legible, for the humans building them and the agents running alongside.

Mermaid AI brings code, a visual canvas, and AI into one editor. And with Mermaid Flow (beta), your workflows don't just describe a process. They run it.

Built on Mermaid.js, the open-source standard with 90k+ GitHub stars.

# Breakthrough AI Operators

Breakthrough AI Operators is a podcast about how the best startup founders are reinventing how their companies work. Not AI hype. Not vendor pitches. Real operators who've rebuilt significant parts of their business around AI — and can talk honestly about what worked and what didn't. Hosted by Roland Siebelink and Doug Miller, co-founders of Midstage Accelerator (7 unicorns built between them, 100+ leadership teams scaled), each episode features a founder who's achieved a genuine step-change breakthrough in how their company operates. These aren't productivity wins or tool adoption stories — they're companies that are structurally different because of AI. # Kaleidos cierra una ronda seed de 2,2 M€ liderada por Athos Capital 

 20 

 jul 2021 

 Indra Kishinchand López 

La empresa tecnológica Kaleidos ha cerrado una ronda de 2'2 millones de euros liderada por el fondo de venture capital Athos Capital. En la operación también ha entrado el CDTI y repiten business angels como Vicente Olivenza, Carlos Cosín, Rafa Garrido y Ricky Posner. Kaleidos, especializada el desarrollo de proyectos basados en software libre para grandes organizaciones y startups tecnológicas de ámbito nacional e internacional, celebra esta semana su décimo aniversario. 

Con esta entrada de capital, Kaleidos se prepara para afrontar un punto de inflexión en su trayectoria. Tras diez años como proveedor de consultoría y servicios digitales, comienza una nueva etapa en la que pondrá el foco en el desarrollo y optimización de sus propios productos. Lo hará concretamente en Taiga (solución para la gestión de proyectos ágiles) y Penpot (plataforma para el diseño y producción de prototipos y UX en un entorno multiusuario). El objetivo es convertirse en tres años en un referente a nivel mundial en herramientas open source para equipos digitales multifuncionales.

# Spain backs open-source design tool Penpot in €6.9M round

● Jul 2026

What's the deal? Kaleidos, the Madrid company behind open-source interface design platform Penpot, has raised €6.9 million in an early VC round. The Sociedad Española para la Transformación Tecnológica (SETT), a public body under Spain's Ministry for Digital Transformation and the Civil Service, contributed €1.92 million.

What does Penpot do? It is an open-source platform for designing and building user interfaces. Its pitch: the first design tool serving both designers and developers, treating design as code — a structure it says suits generative AI natively.

Why now? The most-used interface design platform is controlled by a single US company that holds designs, data, and development considered sensitive intellectual property. SETT frames its investment as a push for European technological sovereignty in a field dependent on foreign firms.

What's the endgame? The funding will let Kaleidos scale its commercial team and paid product. SETT made the investment through its Next Tech facility, using money from Spain's Recovery, Transformation and Resilience Plan, drawn from the EU's Next Generation funds.

## Valuation

In April 2026, Coder raised a [$90 million](https://coder.com/blog/90m-series-c-led-by-kkr-to-advance-secure-enterprise-ai-development) Series C led by KKR, with participation from Qube Research & Technologies (QRT) and existing investor Uncork Capital. Both KKR and QRT are Coder customers, with KKR deploying Coder across more than [500 engineers](https://coder.com/blog/90m-series-c-led-by-kkr-to-advance-secure-enterprise-ai-development) and QRT running it for half of its more than [2K employees](https://coder.com/blog/90m-series-c-led-by-kkr-to-advance-secure-enterprise-ai-development). Coder did not disclose a valuation for the round. One unverified estimate put its post-money valuation after the April 2026 round at [$828 million](https://www.crunchbase.com/organization/coder). As of October 2026, Coder had raised a total of [$172.8 million](https://www.crunchbase.com/organization/coder) in funding.

The Series C followed a [$35 million](https://coder.com/newsroom/press-releases/coder-announces-35m-in-series-b2-funding-to-modernize-the-enterprise-development) Series B extension round in June 2024, led by Georgian, with participation from existing investors Uncork Capital, Notable Capital, and Redpoint Ventures, at an undisclosed valuation. Before that, Coder raised a [$30 million](https://news.crunchbase.com/news/austin-based-coder-raises-30m-for-cloud-based-software-development/) Series B in April 2020, led by GGV Capital, with participation from In-Q-Tel, a non-profit investment firm the CIA set up in [1999](https://www.iqt.org/about) to bring commercial technology to US national security agencies. That April 2020 round reportedly valued Coder at about [$200 million](https://news.crunchbase.com/news/austin-based-coder-raises-30m-for-cloud-based-software-development/).

Prior to this, Coder raised an [$8.4 million](https://news.crunchbase.com/news/austin-based-coder-raises-30m-for-cloud-based-software-development/) Series A led by Redpoint Ventures in 2019, and a [$4.5 million](https://www.newswire.com/news/coder-4-5m-series-seed-announcement-20708080) seed round in November 2018, co-led by Uncork Capital and Redpoint Ventures, with Founders Fund and Capital Factory participating. More than four years passed between the Series B and the subsequent round, which Coder raised in June 2024 as an extension that brought its Series B total to [$65 million](https://coder.com/newsroom/press-releases/coder-announces-35m-in-series-b2-funding-to-modernize-the-enterprise-development), and the Series C followed less than two years later as bookings accelerated.

## Key Opportunities

### Sovereign Infrastructure Mandates

Governments and regulators are pushing enterprises to keep software infrastructure under local control. More than [75%](https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2025/10/23/gartner-2026-technology-trends/) of European and Middle Eastern enterprises are projected to move virtual workloads to local options such as sovereign clouds, regional providers, or their own data centers by 2030 to reduce geopolitical risk, up from less than [5%](https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2025/10/23/gartner-2026-technology-trends/) in 2025.

Effective January 2025, the EU's Digital Operational Resilience Act [requires](https://www.eiopa.europa.eu/digital-operational-resilience-act-dora_en) banks, insurers, and other financial entities to [manage](https://www.cssf.lu/en/ict-and-cyber-risk-for-dora-entities/) the risk of their third-party information and communication technology providers. In June 2025, Microsoft [announced](https://blogs.microsoft.com/blog/2025/06/16/announcing-comprehensive-sovereign-solutions-empowering-european-organizations/) a Sovereign Private Cloud designed to run in hybrid or air-gapped environments. As compute moves into these regional and isolated environments, the AI coding agents that run on top of it have to be deployable there too, which a tool offered only as a vendor-hosted service cannot do. Coder already [supports](https://coder.com/docs/install/airgap) air-gapped and offline deployments, and it plans to use part of its [$90 million](https://coder.com/blog/90m-series-c-led-by-kkr-to-advance-secure-enterprise-ai-development) Series C to expand across Europe, Asia, and North America.

### Governing Agents Beyond Engineering

Identity systems built for human employees and static service accounts are struggling to keep pace with AI agents. A February 2026 industry survey found that more than [16%](https://cloudsecurityalliance.org/blog/2026/02/18/token-sprawl-in-the-age-of-ai) of organizations do not track the creation of new AI-related identities and that [24%](https://cloudsecurityalliance.org/blog/2026/02/18/token-sprawl-in-the-age-of-ai) take more than 24 hours to rotate or revoke a credential after potential exposure.

Coder's customers are already extending it past engineering. In April 2026, KKR [said](https://coder.com/blog/90m-series-c-led-by-kkr-to-advance-secure-enterprise-ai-development) it was extending Coder to analysts, data scientists, and other non-engineering users, and QRT had rolled Coder out to half of its more than [2K employees](https://coder.com/blog/90m-series-c-led-by-kkr-to-advance-secure-enterprise-ai-development), a mix of engineers, data scientists, and analysts. As of October 2026, Coder's agents page [frames](https://coder.com/solutions/agents) AI use as already spanning marketing managers, designers, product managers, financial analysts, and HR leaders.

Coder's architecture is suited to this shift because it avoids creating a new credential type to govern. The agent loop [runs](https://coder.com/docs/ai-coder/agents) in the control plane, LLM credentials never enter the workspace, and every agent action is tied to the authenticated user who submitted the prompt. The agent has the same permissions as that user, with no shared bot identity or service account. An analyst's agent has analyst-level access, and an HR manager’s agent has HR-lev

Devs often rely on local environments — i.e. their laptops — to write, build and test code before shipping it to a cloud service to integrate and deploy it. There’s nothing wrong with that approach. # Qdrant raises $50 Million Series B to define composable vector search as core infrastructure for production AI

 12 March 2026 November 4th, 2026 5 min read 

As AI systems scale into critical operations, enterprises are standardizing on retrieval infrastructure built for control, performance, and flexibility

BERLIN & NEW YORK — March 12, 2026 — Qdrant, the open-source vector search engine built in Rust for production workloads, today announced $50 million in Series B funding led by AVP, with participation from Bosch Ventures, Unusual Ventures, Spark Capital, and 42CAP.

Vector search began as a solution to a narrow problem: retrieving nearest neighbors from dense embeddings over relatively static datasets. Today’s AI systems look nothing like that. Retrieval runs within agent loops, executing thousands of queries per workflow across hybrid modalities, against data that changes continuously. def cite_page(label,author,date=None):
 x=pages[label];url=x['url']
 if url in used:return url
 title=x['text'].splitlines()[0].strip()
 title=title.replace('&',r'\&').replace('%',r'\%').replace('_',r'\_').replace('#',r'\#')
 key='audit'+str(len(used)+1)
 bib=f'@online{{{key},\n author = {{{{{author}}}}},\n title = {{{title}}},\n url = {{{url}}},\n urldate = {{2026-11-26}},\n'
 if date:bib+=f' date = {{{date}}},\n'
 bib+='}\n';save_citation(bib)
 used[url]={'title':title,'url':url,'full_text':x['text'],'author':author,'publishedDate':date,'key':key}
 Path('audit_work/used_sources.json').write_text(json.dumps(used,indent=2,default=str));return url

China’s DeepSeek Swells Investor Base in Second Fundraiser

Liu Xiaojie

DATE: Nov 20 2026

/ SOURCE: Yicai

![China’s DeepSeek Swells Investor Base in Second Fundraiser](https://img.yicaiglobal.com/src/image/2026/11/136360908261061.jpg) China’s DeepSeek Swells Investor Base in Second Fundraiser

(Yicai) Nov. 20 -- DeepSeek’s long-awaited second external fundraiser has greatly expanded the Chinese artificial intelligence developer’s investor base, bringing in more major technology companies, industrial groups, and venture capital firms as its backers.

Investors linked with Tencent, Contemporary Amperex Technology, China Mobile, China Telecom, and Xiaohongshu, as well as financiers like Monolith Capital, Boyu Capital, IDG Capital, Gaorong Capital, and Legend Capital have backed Hangzhou Chengyan Enterprise Management Consulting Partnership, the investment vehicle for the Series B fundraiser with a 17.3 percent stake in DeepSeek after the round, according to data from corporate information site Qichacha.

In addition, the registered capital of Hangzhou DeepSeek Artificial Intelligence Basic Technology Research, the AI startup’s operating entity, rose to CNY19.9 million from around CNY16.5 million (USD3 million from USD2.5 million).

The corporate information changes do not provide information on the amount raised. Media reports have said DeepSeek initially targeted CNY50 billion (USD7.5 billion), then doubled that to roughly CNY100 billion on strong investor demand. The round reportedly closed at about CNY105.5 billion, giving DeepSeek a post-money valuation of around CNY615.5 billion (USD92 billion), making it the largest venture financing ever secured by a Chinese AI firm.

Hangzhou-based DeepSeek has yet to announce any details about the funding round, including the amount raised.

DeepSeek's Series A fundraiser closed in June, raising roughly CNY50 billion. Its backers then included founder Liang Wenfeng, major tech companies such as Tencent, CATL, and NetEase, along with IDG Capital and China’s national AI fund.

In less than a year, DeepSeek has gone from being a geek team driven by tech idealism into an AI unicorn potentially valued at more than CNY600 billion and backed by a broad cross-section of Chinese businesses and investors.

Entities affiliated with Tencent and three investment funds backed by CATL each pitched in about 9.6 percent to the funding round, ranking as the largest contributors among Hangzhou Chengyan's shareholders. The pair were also key external investors in the Series A fundraiser.

The third- to fifth-largest contributors were China Mobile and an entity under Citic Securities, each adding around 7.7percent, followed by Monolith at 7.2 percent.

The funding round also drew participation from entities linked to internet giants such as Meituan, NetEase, and Trip.Com; businesses in the telecoms, devices, and manufacturing sectors like Vivo, Midea, Geely, Luxshare Precision, and GigaDevice; as well as VC firms CPE Yuanfeng, Loyal Valley Capital, and Shixiang Capital.

The privately held company stormed onto the global AI stage in January last year with the release of its ChatGPT-style R1 large language model, which paired strong reasoning performance with dramatically lower running costs, in what Silicon Valley venture capitalist Marc Andreessen famously described as an “AI Sputnik moment.”

With capital and resources now largely in place, the market’s attention is turning to how DeepSeek can maintain its technological edge while delivering commercial results for its investors that are commensurate with its valuation.

Editors: Tang Shihua, Martin Kadiev

## Company evidence, exact excerpts and conflicts

### 1. Textualize

**Status: shut_down.** The founder's [May 2025 announcement](https://textual.textualize.io/blog/2025/05/07/the-future-of-textualize/) states: “we weren't able to find a shared problem or pain-point to build a viable business around. Which is why Textualize, the company, will be wrapping up in the next few weeks.” It separately states: “Textual will live on as an Open Source project.” Continuing repository activity therefore does not establish continuing company operations.

**Financing:** The founder's [Weeknotes](https://www.willmcgugan.com/blog/tech/post/weeknotes/) states: “The investment for Textualize landed at the end of last year, just before Christmas.” No amount is supplied, so funding remains blank.

**Date conflict:** [PitchBook](https://pitchbook.com/profiles/company/510364-36) dates its “Out of Business” event to February 2026. The CSV instead uses the founder's operational wind-down announcement month. The exact completion date and legal dissolution date were not established.

### 2. OtterMind

**Status: private, operating; corporate attribution requires caution.** The [GitHub organization](https://github.com/ottermind) connects OtterMind with Chat2DB and the OtterMind website. The company's [About page](https://ottermind.ai/about) states: “Ottermind is operated by the Singapore-registered company listed here,” identifying **OTTERMIND PTE. LTD.** Its current site markets an operating AI-agent workspace.

**Financing conflict:** The [36Kr Chat2DB profile](https://pitchhub.36kr.com/project/3173327576230918) instead identifies the Chinese legal entity **爱獭科技（杭州）有限公司**, translated there as Love Otter Technology (Hangzhou) Co., Ltd. Its financing table lists angel, Series A and Series A+ events, with the latest in May 2026, but the amount field is **“未透露”**, meaning “undisclosed.” I did not establish whether these financings belong to the Singapore entity, an affiliate, or another corporate perimeter. No amount or valuation was transferred into OtterMind's row.

### 3. HeroUI Inc.

**Status: private, operating.** [Y Combinator's company page](https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/heroui) says “Status: Active” and identifies Junior Garcia as “Founder and CEO of HeroUI (formerly NextUI).”

**Verified investment, undisclosed amount:** Investor Epakon's [annual review](https://blog.epakon.com/uncovering-opportunities-a-look-back-and-ahead-at-a-thrilling-year-in-vc-ac7b1d446fda) states: “In 2023, Epakon led NextUI’s pre-seed round.” It does not give the investment amount.

**Excluded conflicting figures:** The search-index financial panel associated with the [LinkedIn profile](https://linkedin.com/company/heroui) says “Total Funding: USD 425,000,” whereas [aVenture](https://aventure.vc/companies/heroui-san-francisco-ca-us/fundraising) says “Disclosed Funding$500,000.” Neither was established as an authoritative company-specific funding announcement. I also did not substitute Y Combinator's generic investment terms. Total funding remains blank.

### 4. Chatwoot

**Status: private, operating.** Its [current commercial website](https://www.chatwoot.com/) offers the hosted customer-support product and enterprise services.

**Accepted funding: USD 1,600,000.** The company's [investor handbook](https://www.chatwoot.com/hc/handbook/articles/investors-27) states: “We raised a $1.6M seed round from Goat Capital, Uncorrelated Ventures & YCombinator.” [VentureBeat's announcement](https://venturebeat.com/business/chatwoot-challenges-zendesk-with-open-source-customer-engagement-platform), dated August 2021, independently says Chatwoot “today announced it has raised $1.6 million in seed funding.” This establishes `funding_asof=2021-08`.

**Conflict:** [PitchBook](https://pitchbook.com/profiles/company/227991-43) says: “Chatwoot has raised $1.91M,” and lists a different seed-round amount. I preferred the company's explicit disclosure. The CSV total represents the disclosed company-backed round, not independently audited lifetime proceeds. No generic accelerator cheque was added separately because the company already includes Y Combinator among the round's investors.

### 5. Typst GmbH

**Status: private, operating.** Its [current About page](https://typst.app/about/) describes the company and commercial platform. Founder Martin Haug's [company update](https://typst.app/blog/2025/future/) states: “As a company, we have grown financially sustainable over the past two years.”

**Financing:** [EWOR's Typst profile](https://www.ewor.com/startups/typst) identifies Martin Haug as a fellow and describes the business, but discloses no investment amount. Typst's [statement about Posit](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/typst_posit-and-typst-posit-activity-7342823256472584192-pyUB) says: “Their commitment to funding one of our full-time engineers means the world to us.” That establishes development sponsorship, not a disclosed equity round or valuation. No numerical equity total was verified.

### 6. NanoCo

**Status: private, operating, not acquired.** The [current company website](https://www.nanoco.ai/) offers enterprise AI assistants and early access.

**Accepted funding: USD 12,000,000.** The [company's announcement](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/nanoclaw-ai_today-were-announcing-nanoco-creators-of-activity-7462949209873235969-gMOs) states: “Today we're announcing NanoCo (creators of NanoClaw), our enterprise offering from the team behind NanoClaw, and a $12M seed round led by Valley Capital Partners.” [TechCrunch](https://techcrunch.com/2026/05/20/nanoclaw-creator-turns-down-20m-buyout-offer-raises-12m-seed-instead/), dated May 2026, confirms an “oversubscribed $12 million seed round.”

**Important exclusion:** TechCrunch reports “a roughly $20 million acquisition offer” that the founders “declined.” An unconsummated offer, reportedly including employment arrangements, is neither an exit value nor a disclosed post-money financing valuation. All valuation and exit fields remain blank.

### 7. usablica (Intro.js)

**Status: private commercial operation, with legal-entity uncertainty.** The [official website](https://introjs.com/) states: “Free for open-source projects. A once-off payment for commercial ones.” Its footer identifies Usablica. This supports continuing paid licensing rather than shutdown.

No equity amount, valuation or acquisition announcement was located. The incorporation jurisdiction and exact legal entity behind the brand were not independently established; `private` describes the continuing independent commercial operation, not a verified corporate-registration finding.

### 8. LiteFold

**Status: private, operating.** The [current website](https://www.litefold.ai/) identifies “LiteFold Inc., a Delaware C-Corporation” and markets its private AI platform.

**Undisclosed equity; grants excluded.** [YourStory](https://yourstory.com/2026/05/litefold-biotech-startup-using-proprietary-ai-speed-up-drug-discovery) states: “The startup recently raised an undisclosed amount in a private funding round led by Offscript VC.” It continues: “It has also secured about $23,000 in grants from Emergent Ventures, Dr Aniruddha Malpani’s 3F VC, and also an undisclosed friends and family round from the Boston-based OffScript VC.”

The wording does not clearly establish whether the private and friends-and-family descriptions refer to separate transactions. I did not double-count them or enter grants as equity. The same article states: “Sannigrahi later shifted it into a proprietary platform after recognising the commercial potential of the technology,” which is relevant to the supplied open-source classification.

### 9. AIPOCH

**Status: private, operating.** Its [company-issued PR Newswire release](https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/aipoch-launches-open-science-making-research-easier-to-follow-learn-from-and-share-with-science-packages-302908207.html), dated October 2026 and issued from Singapore, states: “AIPOCH today announced the formal public release of AIPOCH Open-Science.”

The release establishes recent operations but discloses no equity financing, valuation or acquisition price. No such financial disclosure was located in the bounded search.

### 10. MeshPro

**Status: private commercial operation; supplied entity is a product name.** [Monday Tech's official documentation](https://mondaytech.com/meshpro/getting-started/) states: “MeshPro is a collection of Python libraries and command-line tools for mesh I/O and mesh manipulation.” It adds: “Full access to all MeshPro functionality requires a license.”

The [optimesh repository](https://github.com/meshpro/optimesh) directs commercial users to **support@mondaytech.com**. This supports ongoing commercialization under Monday Tech, but not a separately incorporated company called MeshPro or a completed acquisition. No funding amount or valuation was located. I retained the supplied entity label and flagged the identity issue rather than inventing a buyer or acquisition event.

### 11. Yunnan BinaryStars Technologies

**Status: private, operating.** The company's [About page](https://www.binarystarstech.com/en/about/) describes its integrated hardware and software engineering business and links the Borneo-IoT product line. The [Borneo-IoT app terms](https://www.borneoiot.com/app/tos/), updated March 2026, identify the service as “operated by Yunnan BinaryStars Technologies, Co., Ltd.”

No disclosed equity amount, valuation or acquisition price was found. The terms retain some unfilled template placeholders elsewhere; I used only their explicit operator identification, corroborated by the company website.

## Uncertain rows and interpretation

The principal uncertainties are **OtterMind**'s corporate relationship to the Chinese Chat2DB business; **HeroUI**'s conflicting unsupported funding totals; **Usablica**'s and **MeshPro**'s legal-entity identities; **LiteFold**'s ambiguous round descriptions; and **Textualize**'s exact cessation date. Chatwoot's reported database total also conflicts with its own disclosure. None of these uncertainties was resolved by inventing a number.

No qualifying post-money valuation, completed acquisition price, or first-day public-market capitalization was verified for these companies. Consequently, every valuation and exit-value field is blank. No currency conversion was necessary for the accepted funding figures.

## Saved files and reproduction

All files below concern the public-disclosure snapshot as of 2026-11-26; genome builds and scientific dataset releases are not applicable.

- `/workspace/downloads/oss_financial_disclosures/financial_disclosures.csv`: Analysis-ready curated data. Sources are the company, investor and news URLs above. Transformations were entity matching, status classification, exclusion of grants and uncompleted offers, and conversion of explicit USD million amounts into integer USD digits. Validated for 11 rows, exact columns, integer-or-blank financial fields and notes of at most 25 words.
- `/workspace/downloads/oss_financial_disclosures/evidence.json`: Supporting original tool-returned search and fetched-page text, all retrieval queries and URLs, and used-source metadata. Retrieval used `e14c.web.web_search` with five results per query and `e14c.web.fetch_parsed_page` on the recorded HTTPS URLs. Results were serialized without financial estimation.
- `/workspace/downloads/oss_financial_disclosures/sources.bib`: Supporting hand-curated bibliographic metadata for the 29 sources cited below. Source URLs and publication dates are retained when available.
- `/workspace/downloads/oss_financial_disclosures/methodology.json`: Supporting research parameters, screening definitions, conflicts, call counts and validation findings. Derived from the saved evidence and curation decisions.
- `/workspace/downloads/oss_financial_disclosures/reproduce_retrieval.py`: Repeats the exact retrieval calls recorded in `evidence.json`; run with `python /workspace/downloads/oss_financial_disclosures/reproduce_retrieval.py`. It does not substitute automated extraction for the documented manual financial judgments.

The same bibliography was also saved through `save_citation` to `/workspace/citations/default_project/08d1321c-1746-402b-bad9-7f630a43bf59.bib`. Complete bibliography follows so the caller does not need filesystem access.
